problem: The closing line says additives change behaviour 'not its basic viscosity', but the same section has just explained that a VI improver raises hot viscosity — the very property a grade is built on. A student will read the two statements as contradictory.
fix: The base oil supplies most of the volume and the bulk of the viscosity; additives modify its behaviour — some, like VI improvers, deliberately shift the measured viscosity at given temperatures — but they do not replace the base oil.

where: Section 1, grade description (also Quiz Q2 answer)
problem: The W part of a grade is described only as a cold-cranking limit, and the 40 part only as a kinematic-viscosity band at 100 °C. A full SAE grade also fixes a low-temperature pumping (MRV) limit, a minimum kinematic viscosity at 100 °C for the W part, and a high-temperature high-shear (HTHS) minimum. Calling it a single cold-cranking limit understates the definition.
fix: The 10W part sets low-temperature limits — a cold-cranking (CCS) limit and a pumping (MRV) limit — plus a minimum kinematic viscosity at 100 °C; the 40 part is a kinematic-viscosity band at 100 °C together with a high-temperature high-shear (HTHS) minimum. A multigrade oil meets both sets.
